title: The Harlem Renaissance
objective: After this level you can explain how Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston brought Black speech and music into American literature.
summary: In the Harlem Renaissance, Langston Hughes wrote poems to the rhythm of blues and jazz, and Zora Neale Hurston collected Eatonville's folklore and wrote Their Eyes Were Watching God in its speech.

cards.headline: A poem that sways like a blues piano.
cards.body: "Droning a drowsy syncopated tune, / Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon," So begins "The Weary Blues", the title poem of Langston Hughes's first book, published in 1926. Hughes became a fixture of the Harlem Renaissance, the 1920s flowering that celebrated African American culture and achievement. His idea: let the poem move like the music.

cards.headline: The blues on the page
cards.body: Hughes said the people he met were the influences of his work, but blues and jazz were its rhythm. He wanted to tell his people's stories the way they actually lived them, with their music, laughter and language. Among his main influences he named Walt Whitman. You met Whitman's long, crowded lines in Level 75; Hughes filled that American song with Black voices.

cards.headline: An anthropologist on her own front porch
cards.body: Zora Neale Hurston grew up in Eatonville, Florida, incorporated in 1887 as one of the nation's first Black towns. On the porch of the village store, she heard people spin colorful stories. At Barnard College she studied anthropology with Franz Boas, then went home to Florida to collect folklore. The result, Mules and Men (1935), put Black Southern folklore in print.

cards.fact: In her great novel, every character talks the way the rural South talked.
cards.context: In Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Hurston's narration is in standard English, but every character speaks Southern African American Vernacular English, and much of the book's energy comes from the contrast. The porch talk she grew up hearing became the voice of a novel.
